extracted.intended_audience: policy officials and advisers in New Zealand government agencies preparing regulatory proposals and Regulatory Impact Assessments (RIAs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for New Zealand government agencies on meeting Cabinet’s Impact Analysis Requirements when developing regulatory proposals, including preparing Regulatory Impact Assessments, obtaining independent Quality Assurance, applying for exemptions, and publishing final material. Focused on the practical steps, templates, processes and quality criteria needed for Cabinet consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide a Regulatory Impact Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact Analysis is required for any government policy initiative that includes consideration of regulatory options (that is, options that will ultimately create, amend, or repeal primary or secondary legislation). Cabinet papers that include a regulatory proposal must be accompanied by a Regulatory Impact Assessment, unless an exemption applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes enabling legislation, cost recovery proposals, discussion documents that include options that may lead to regulatory change, “in principle” policy decisions, negotiating mandates for treaties with regulatory impacts, and informing Cabinet of a Minister’s decision to make secondary legislation. If amendments to a bill occur later, update the RIA to indicate how changes affect the Impact Analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of Impact Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of Impact Analysis is to improve the quality of policy by ensuring that policy proposals are subject to careful and robust analysis. Impact Analysis is intended to provide assurance about whether problems might be adequately addressed through private or non-regulatory arrangements—and to ensure that particular policy solutions have been demonstrated to enhance the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework encourages a systematic and evidence‑informed approach to policy development and contributes to transparency and accountability through routine publication of RIAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying problem or opportunity is properly identified, and is supported by available evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on operational intelligence and available monitoring or review information. Avoid incomplete problem definitions which are a frequent cause of inadequate Impact Analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options identification (including non‑regulatory options)
rubrics_metrics.description: All practical options to address the problem or opportunity have been considered, including alternative legislative and non‑legislative policy options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how proposed options interact or align with existing domestic and international requirements within this or related regulatory systems. Ensure options are not narrowed prematurely and document the reasons for rejecting options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact and risk analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: All material impacts and risks of proposed actions have been identified and assessed in a consistent way, including possible unintended consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a genuine effort to identify, understand and estimate the various categories of cost and benefit associated with the options; assess uncertainty and risks, and consider distributional, social, economic and environmental impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear rationale for recommended option
rubrics_metrics.description: It is clear why a particular option has been recommended over others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain trade‑offs, evidence basis, and how the recommended option delivers best on objectives compared with alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess importance within regulatory systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the importance of the issue in relation to the overall performance and condition of the relevant regulatory system(s), and how it might fit with plans, priorities or opportunities for system improvement already identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider system‑level objectives, stewardship responsibilities and potential interactions with other regulatory measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify nature and underlying cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly identify the nature and underlying cause of the policy or operational problem to be addressed, drawing on operational intelligence and available monitoring or review information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish symptoms from root causes; use evidence and monitoring data where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate and present costs and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a genuine effort to identify, understand, and estimate the various categories of cost and benefit associated with the options for change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established guidance and tools (eg, Treasury Cost Benefit Analysis guidance). Where monetisation is not possible, describe and quantify impacts qualitatively and transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation design, resourcing and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and address practical design, resourcing and timing issues required for effective implementation and operation, in conjunction with the regulator(s) who will be expected to deliver and administer the changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider feasibility, administrative costs, transitional arrangements, enforcement and ongoing monitoring, and ensure implementation risks are assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement and consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide affected and interested parties with appropriate opportunities to comment throughout the process and, in the right circumstances, to participate directly in the regulatory design process (co‑design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Guidance Note: Effective consultation for Impact Analysis. Consultation design should be structured around the Impact Analysis framework and include suitable questions for stakeholders. Consultation quality is part of QA assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open‑book scrutiny for proposed charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of “open‑book” exercises to allow potential fee or levy paying parties to scrutinise the case for, and structure and level of, proposed statutory charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open‑book exercises support transparency and help justify cost‑recovery arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early engagement with Treasury and QA panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek early feedback from Treasury and Quality Assurance panels on initial problem definition and likely options, ideally both after tentative decisions to pursue action and before committing to a particular approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Early Engagement for Impact Analysis Form (or equivalent) and indicate your timeframe. Early engagement can save time later by identifying gaps and helping reviewers plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard templates and required content
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the appropriate Regulatory Impact Assessment template and include the required content, consultation and circulation, manager sign‑off and agency disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard templates and supporting forms are available on Treasury's Regulation webpage. Agree any departures from templates with the Regulatory Quality Team in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for exemption — technical or case‑specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals do not require a Regulatory Impact Assessment if they meet any of these technical or case‑specific conditions: 1) suitable for inclusion in a revision Bill; 2) suitable for inclusion in a Statutes Amendment Bill; 3) would repeal or remove redundant legislative provisions; 4) provides solely for the commencement of existing legislation or legislative provisions; 5) solely a request to authorise spending in Appropriation or Imprest Supply bills; 6) solely a request to confirm secondary legislation that has already been made; 7) implements deeds of settlement for Treaty of Waitangi claims, other than those that would amend or affect existing regulatory arrangements; 8) brings into effect recognition agreements under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011; 9) essential (the minimum necessary) in order to comply with existing international obligations that are binding on New Zealand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exemptions relate to particular circumstances and include technical adjustments, transitional arrangements and non‑substantive changes. The Regulatory Quality Team grants exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for exemption — minor impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory proposals that have no impacts, or only minor impacts, on businesses, individuals or not‑for‑profit entities do not require a Regulatory Impact Assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meaning of “no or minor impacts” is subjective and decided by the Regulatory Quality Team based on agency information. Typical cases include technical administrative adjustments, internal government transfers, codifying existing practice, localised impacts, or low Net Present Value over the medium term. The exemption is unlikely where impacts are regional/national, substantially alter regulatory system objectives, change legal rights/responsibilities of agencies, or affect public‑facing policy processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for exemption — discretionary
rubrics_metrics.description: A RIA may not be required where formal Impact Analysis is not the best and most cost‑effective way to ensure Ministers have access to relevant information, and the proposal fits one of: i) the relevant issues have already been adequately addressed by existing Impact Analysis; ii) a RIA would substantively duplicate other government policy development, reporting and publication requirements or commitments; iii) the government has limited statutory decision making discretion or responsibility for the content of proposed delegated legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary exemptions are granted subject to conditions (eg, incorporating elements of the IA framework into a discussion document or Better Business Case). Treasury will discuss conditions and timing with the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying for an exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: If you consider an exemption may apply, apply to the Regulatory Quality Team (ria@treasury.govt.nz) using the Exemption Application Form or equivalent, stating the exemption sought and why it applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treasury considers the information, may request clarification, and will determine the extent of any exemption and conditions. Copy your Treasury policy team into correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation of RIA process (template and QA responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treasury determines the appropriate RIA template and whether your agency or Treasury is responsible for arranging independent Quality Assurance, based on information you provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions consider agency policy capability, internal QA robustness, regulatory stewardship strength, robustness of planned policy process, significance of likely impacts, and levels of risk and uncertainty. Use the Process Confirmation Form and advise Treasury if circumstances change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreeing departures from templates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulatory Quality Team may agree on a case‑by‑case basis to depart from the standard RIA templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If standard templates are unsuitable, discuss alternatives with the Regulatory Quality Team and agree the approach early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent Quality Assurance requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain independent Quality Assurance for your Regulatory Impact Assessment; Quality Assurance assessors provide an independent assessment of the RIA's overall quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QA arrangements vary; the RIA must meet the QA criteria. QA can be arranged by Treasury or the agency as confirmed. QA assessors should be independent from authors and focus on the nature, quality and robustness of analysis rather than advocacy for a proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should undertake Quality Assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality Assurance should be undertaken by persons or panels that are independent and suitably skilled to assess the analysis and evidence in the RIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include internal agency QA panels, central assesors in Treasury, or external specialists. Choice depends on significance, complexity and agency capability. QA arrangements should be proportionate to risk and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Quality Assurance involves
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality Assurance involves assessing whether the RIA meets Cabinet’s Impact Analysis Requirements, including the adequacy of problem definition, options considered, analysis of impacts and risks, consultation, and evidence supporting conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QA assessors may provide early comments on draft material, indicate likely final assessment, highlight gaps, and preserve independence in the final statement. QA statements should indicate whether the RIA meets, partially meets, or does not meet the criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing a Quality Assurance statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality Assurance assessors must prepare an independent Quality Assurance statement to be included in the Cabinet paper providing an independent assessment of the overall quality of the RIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements should set out the assessment of the RIA against the QA criteria and any conditions or caveats. They should be clear, evidence‑based and proportionate to the significance of the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and review of QA practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Quality Assurance criteria must be applied consistently across proposals and over time; moderation arrangements could include centralised oversight, peer review, rotating responsibilities, and periodic independent review of samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should maintain a register of RIAs and outcomes and may commission independent sampling or reviews to assure consistent application of QA criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet paper 'Impact Analysis Requirements' section
rubrics_metrics.description: All Cabinet papers must include a section entitled 'Impact Analysis Requirements' to link the RIA and the Cabinet paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an exemption has been granted include Treasury’s exemption statement and any conditions. If no exemption, include: 1) an agency statement that the Impact Analysis Requirements apply and the RIA is attached; and 2) the QA assessor’s independent statement on overall quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling regulatory proposals with inadequate Impact Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact Analysis may be considered inadequate where there is no accompanying RIA and no exemption, or where the RIA has not been independently quality assured or has been assessed as 'does not meet' the QA criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are responsible for early warning. Treasury may advise Ministers. If possible, revise the RIA and re‑assess before lodging; if the paper proceeds with inadequate IA, the Cabinet Committee Chair has discretion whether to consider it and a Supplementary Analysis Report will be required if substantive decisions are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary Analysis Report requirement and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Cabinet paper with inadequate Impact Analysis proceeds and substantive decisions are made, a Supplementary Analysis Report is required to provide Ministers with final reassurance (or otherwise) of the policy approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report should be agreed with the responsible Minister and Minister for Regulatory Reform, reference the particular purpose and stage for which it is required, and may include supplementary analysis (eg, costings, compliance levels, implementation plans), findings from consultation on exposure drafts, commitments to post‑implementation review, and a commitment to publish the original Cabinet paper. Supplementary Reports are subject to QA and must be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing RIAs and Supplementary Analysis Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The full text of all RIAs and Supplementary Analysis Reports must be published on the websites of both the administering Agency and Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deletions consistent with the Official Information Act 1982 are permitted. Timing: publish when any resulting Bill is introduced, any resulting regulation is gazetted, or the government announces its decision not to regulate; agencies may publish earlier at ministerial discretion. Agencies must submit completed publication form and Word versions to the Regulatory Quality Team and comply with NZ Government Web Standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process details for publication and parliamentary material
rubrics_metrics.description: When RIAs are due for publication agencies must send publication forms and Word versions to the Regulatory Quality Team; provide web URLs to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) to include in Explanatory Notes; provide forty printed copies of the RIA and Supplementary Analysis Report for Bills to the Bills Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must keep Treasury informed about timing of introduction/gazettal so Treasury can publish promptly. PCO will provide standard wording for URL text and agencies must supply designated URLs in time for printed drafts to LEG.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure statements for proposed legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must disclose in a standalone statement the Quality Assurance processes they have undertaken during the development of legislation, and key features of that legislation that are likely to be of interest to the public and Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure statement is separate from the RIA, largely takes the form of YES/NO questions with elaboration where required, and links to existing government expectations for legislation development. See Detailed Guide to Disclosure Statements for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning and continuous improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from previous Quality Assurance processes and build those lessons into future policy processes and projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ex‑post quality assessment, peer review and QA panels; embed lessons via agency policy quality assessment processes and tools such as the Policy Project's Start Right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start Right / early validation and testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Policy Project’s Start Right tools to assist policy practitioners to consider important drivers of policy quality early, including validation and testing activities relevant to assessing the policy problem/opportunity and key assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start Right is compatible with the Impact Analysis process; for regulatory policy, Impact Analysis is the primary manifestation of validation and testing activities.
